nature-res-111.title: Virtual water: the water hidden in what we trade
nature-res-111.text: A tonne of beef carries, on world average, 15,497 cubic meters of water, against 1,334 for a tonne of wheat. That hidden water is virtual water, also called embedded or embodied water. It is the water used to make food and other goods, which in effect moves from place to place when those goods are traded. Tony Allan coined the concept in 1993 and won the Stockholm Water Prize for it in 2008. The logic is simple. A country that imports one tonne of wheat instead of growing it saves about 1,300 cubic meters of its own water. Water-scarce Israel discourages exporting oranges, which need a lot of water, to avoid shipping its water abroad. Cereal imports can make up for local shortages, but poor countries may not be able to afford them in future. Economists can build virtual water data into trade models such as GTAP to study water policy and trade. The idea has critics. Australia's National Water Commission, among others, says measuring virtual water has little practical value for deciding how to share out scarce water.

nature-res-122.title: Environmental flows: water left for the river
nature-res-122.text: More than half of the world's large rivers are dammed, and dams change downstream water quality, temperature, sediment, fish and livelihoods. Environmental flow is the amount, timing and quality of river flow needed to sustain freshwater and estuarine ecosystems and the people who depend on them. Estuarine means where a river meets the sea. Managers aim for a flow pattern that serves human uses while keeping rivers healthy, not necessarily restoring pristine flows. The idea grew from 1970s 'minimum flows' for single species such as trout, then 'instream flows'. By the 1990s scientists saw that one minimum flow could not capture how rivers work. The 2007 Brisbane Declaration was endorsed by more than 750 practitioners from more than 50 countries. More than 200 methods now exist; holistic ones include DRIFT, the Building Block Methodology and ELOHA. Gains are possible on both sides. Reoperating dams alongside {{ref:nature-nbs-187}} has sometimes increased water for hydropower while reducing flood risk.

nature-res-091.title: Water stress indicators: measuring scarcity with a number
nature-res-091.text: Below 1,700 cubic meters of water per person per year, a country is under water stress; below 1,000, it faces scarcity. That is the Falkenmark Water Stress Indicator, one of several simple measures of how scarce water is. Others compare water use with the water available. The FAO divides total freshwater withdrawn by total renewable freshwater, minus what rivers need to stay healthy. Below 10% counts as low stress, and above 80% as very high. Such numbers have limits. Country averages hide uneven rainfall and access, so they can misstate scarcity.

nature-res-105.title: The Dublin Principles: water as an economic good
nature-res-105.text: In 1992 a statement agreed in Dublin set out four principles for managing water. Fresh water is finite and vulnerable. Its management should be participatory. Women play a central role. The fourth principle broke new ground: water has economic value in all its competing uses and should be recognized as an economic good. Since 1992 the principles have guided reform of national water law around the world.

nature-res-153.title: Reduced-impact logging: cutting with care
nature-res-153.text: Selective logging touches an estimated 1 billion hectares of forest worldwide, including 680 million hectares of tropical forest. It removes only a few species of trees above a minimum size and leaves the rest standing, unlike {{ref:nature-res-115}}. Done badly, by untrained crews cutting too often or too heavily, it ruins the stand, its water functions and its biodiversity. Reduced-impact logging is the answer: carefully planned and controlled harvesting by trained workers. The term arose in the late 1990s, after mechanized logging was seen to threaten long-term sustainability. The FAO's model code calls for a cutting cycle of at least 20 years, removing no more than one-third of the stand's trunk area, and directional felling. It damages fewer trees and less soil, but in Southeast Asia logging more than 8 trees per hectare cancels its benefits. It can earn rewards for keeping carbon in the forest and is an eligible REDD+ activity. Whether it costs loggers money is disputed. Some studies find losses, while others find gains from wasting less timber.

nature-res-106.title: Faustmann's formula: when to cut a forest
nature-res-106.text: Waiting longer gives a bigger tree, but it also delays the next crop. In 1849 German forester {{ref:nature-hist-080}} worked out how to weigh the two. His formula gives the {{ref:nature-econ-762}} of the income from growing and harvesting a forest again and again. It values the forest as pf(T) divided by (exp(rT) − 1): the harvest value at age T over an endless series of rotations, with r the discount rate. Because timber is renewable, delay has a cost. The best time to cut is when the forest's value grows at the rate of interest on the forest plus interest on the land. Bertil Ohlin solved the maximization in 1921, giving the Faustmann–Ohlin theorem. Because it counts the time value of money through {{ref:nature-econ-745}}, the financially best rotation is usually shorter than the biologically best one. The formula remains widely used in natural resource valuation and policy analysis.

nature-res-150.title: Precision agriculture: farming field by field, row by row
nature-res-150.text: Precision agriculture treats a field as many small patches rather than one. It is a farm management strategy that collects and analyzes data on fields, plants and animals to fit decisions to local variation. It applies precise amounts of water, fertilizer and pesticides at the right time, cutting inputs while raising yields. It relies on GPS, mapping software, variable-rate machinery, grid sampling and {{ref:nature-es-057}}. Farmers earn back their investment by saving on inputs, and targeting them also benefits soils and groundwater. The idea first emerged in the United States in the early 1980s.

nature-res-128.title: Alternative food systems: shorter chains, closer links
nature-res-128.text: Farmers' markets, community-supported agriculture, food cooperatives and buying groups share one thing: they bypass the industrial food chain. They are alternative food systems, initiatives that organize growing, distributing and eating food differently. They are marked by locality, short supply chains and direct links between producers and consumers. Fair trade aims to give producers in developing countries more control and a bigger share of the sale price.

nature-res-127.title: Sustainable food systems: feeding people without the damage
nature-res-127.text: Around 69 million hectares a year grow food that is lost or wasted before reaching consumers. A sustainable food system would cut that waste. It provides healthy food while sustaining the environmental, economic and social systems around food. It starts from sustainable farming and distribution, sustainable diets and less food waste. Such systems are argued to be central to many or all of the 17 SDGs, the UN's global development goals.

nature-res-158.title: Coppicing: a forest that regrows from its stumps
nature-res-158.text: Cut down many trees and they do not die; they sprout again. Coppicing is a way of regrowing a forest that relies on that habit. Most hardwoods, the coast redwood and certain pines can be coppiced. It is generally used for fuelwood, pulpwood and other small-tree products. There are three recognized systems: simple coppice, coppice with standards, where some fine trees are kept for several rotations, and the coppice selection system.

nature-res-159.title: Even-aged and uneven-aged forest management
nature-res-159.text: Foresters can cut a stand all at once or a little at a time. Those choices define two broad families of methods for harvesting timber and re-establishing the forest. Even-aged methods remove most or all of the tallest trees, leaving a stand of one age. Uneven-aged methods harvest single trees or small groups now and then, keeping mixed sizes and ages. The shelterwood system removes a stand through several partial cuts over years. Selection systems suit places where continuous forest cover matters most, for scenic or environmental reasons. Variable retention, a newer system, leaves stumps, logs and live trees for at least one rotation.

nature-res-157.title: Forest thinning: fewer trees, faster growth
nature-res-157.text: Sometimes the way to grow more wood is to cut trees down. Forest thinning removes some trees from a stand so the rest grow faster. It controls how much growing space each tree gets, shaping the growth, quality and health of those left. Thinning dense young stands early can greatly raise the yield of saleable wood and shorten the rotation. Repeated thinnings have been shown to store more carbon than clear-cutting on short rotations.

nature-res-124.title: Net animal losses: the calories lost in feeding livestock
nature-res-124.text: Feeding crops to animals loses more food than all conventional food losses combined. Net animal losses measure that: the calories in human-edible crops fed to animals, minus the calories returned as meat, dairy and fish. The measure also shows why counting loss in tonnes misleads. Tonnes ignore economic value and can overweight heavy, low-value products.

nature-res-147.title: Hardin, Ostrom and the fate of shared pastures
nature-res-147.text: In 1968 {{ref:nature-hist-052}} argued that shared grazing land is bound to be overgrazed, a claim at the heart of the {{ref:nature-econ-606}}. He treated pastoralist land use as unstable and a cause of environmental damage, and his paper gave a basis for privatizing land. Many scholars call his assumption that herders cannot talk or make agreements implausible. Yet it shaped development projects that broke up working pastoral governance, often disastrously. {{ref:nature-hist-039}} disputed Hardin's view. She argued that community groups and cooperatives can manage shared pastures more sustainably than privatization or full state control.

nature-res-145.title: Multiple use and sustained yield
nature-res-145.text: On June 12, 1960, a United States law gave national forests five equal jobs: timber, range, water, recreation and wildlife. It was the first law to treat these major uses equally, so timber sales were no longer always the limiting factor. The principle it set is multiple use and sustained yield. Multiple use means managing all of a forest's renewable surface resources in the combination that best meets people's needs. Sustained yield means keeping a high, regular output of those resources forever without harming the land's productivity.

nature-res-138.title: Who pays when the water table falls
nature-res-138.text: As water tables drop, every well must go deeper, and deeper wells cost money. That burden falls unevenly. In Punjab, the cost of deeper wells hurt small landholders more than large ones, who could afford the technology. Water law can deepen the gap. Under {{ref:nature-res-151}}, established, richer users keep their water while newcomers and small farmers get less.

nature-res-173.title: Agricultural economics: economics for the farm
nature-res-173.text: Economists often cite the farm sector as a prime example of perfect competition, many sellers with no power over price. Agricultural economics is the branch of applied economics that uses theory to improve how food and fiber are produced and distributed. It began with land use, aiming to maximize crop yields while keeping soils healthy. It rose to prominence around the turn of the 20th century and made early contributions to statistical methods in economics. Today agricultural economists design incentives to control farm water pollution and other externalities. They also estimate the value of non-market benefits such as attractive rural landscapes.

nature-res-161.title: Saving tropical rainforests, and making it pay
nature-res-161.text: In 2011, 58 countries signed the {{ref:nature-nbs-139}}, pledging to restore 150 million hectares of forest by 2020, later raised to 350 Mha by 2030. Tropical rainforest conservation covers efforts to protect and restore these forests, from strict preservation to sustainable management by the people who live in them. Its building blocks include ecotourism, rehabilitation, replanting and restoration. Approaches differ. Vietnam and China fund planting directly, while Peru and Brazil give farmers incentives such as tax credits to reduce deforestation. Countries can also earn carbon credits by conserving or replanting rainforest, so conservation pays.

nature-res-116.title: Should water be bought and sold?
nature-res-116.text: For most of the 20th century, states supplied water as a public service, with the emphasis on fairness. Then the idea of water as a commodity grew sharply, alongside worries about scarcity and environmental damage. Commodification of water is the process of turning water, especially fresh water, from a {{ref:nature-econ-633}} into a commodity that can be bought and sold. It is usually done in the hope that the resource will be managed more efficiently. Its theoretical case draws on the {{ref:nature-econ-606}}, an argument made by {{ref:nature-hist-052}}: water held in common has been overused and poorly managed. A price aims to bring the costs of using water into economic decisions, on the logic that a correctly valued resource can be protected. Critics reply that the poor lose out, as equality and universal access are traded for efficiency and profit. Karen Bakker argues full commodification is nearly impossible, because water's physical traits resist standardization. The argument is unsettled. Supporters say markets allocate and protect water better than regulation. Critics say commodification deepens inequality and harms ecosystems.

nature-res-164.title: Water privatization: private firms at the tap
nature-res-164.text: Private water companies were common in the 19th century, faded as public utilities grew, and returned in the early 1990s. Lending conditions from the World Bank and IMF helped push the revival. Water privatization is the involvement of private companies in providing water supply and sanitation. It comes in two broad forms. In full privatization, assets are sold permanently; this is now rare, limited to England, Chile and some US cities. In a public–private partnership, the public keeps ownership and hands some functions to a firm for a set period. Either way, a water operator is a {{ref:nature-econ-350}}, so its tariffs, service quality and environmental record need regulating. Supporters say privatization raises efficiency and service quality and can help public budgets. Critics say it raises tariffs and conflicts with the human right to water. The evidence is mixed, and both sides tend to cite the studies that suit them. A World Bank review found no statistically significant difference in efficiency between public and private operators. A study of Latin American concessions found modest returns, averaging 7 percent a year on capital employed.

nature-res-152.title: First in time, first in right, beyond water
nature-res-152.text: Gold Rush miners applied the same rule to gold as to water: whoever first found and mined a deposit gained the legal right to mine it. First-in-time rights reach other resources too, such as farmland and pollution rights. Granting pollution rights to existing polluters, from which a cap-and-trade market could grow, would apply the idea to air. Carbon markets that let firms offset new emissions against cuts at old sources in effect recognize a prior right of existing emitters, as in {{ref:nature-pol-253}}.

nature-res-149.title: Backstop water sources: the expensive last resort
nature-res-149.text: Desalination cost US$0.53 per cubic metre in Israel in 2005 and US$0.49 in Singapore in 2006. Turning seawater fresh is the classic backstop water source: a supply abundant enough to replace unsustainable or non-renewable water use, usually at a higher {{ref:nature-econ-347}}. A backstop plays the role renewable energy plays for fossil fuels. Transfers between river basins and trucked water are others, and all are expensive last resorts. Desalination is limited by its energy needs, brine disposal, high capital and water costs, and the cost of moving water.

nature-res-118.title: Criteria and indicators: scoring forest sustainability
nature-res-118.text: How can a country tell whether its forests are managed sustainably? Criteria and indicators are policy tools for checking and reporting that. Criteria set the objectives; indicators are the variables that show whether they are met. The idea dates to the 1992 {{ref:nature-gov-136}} and {{ref:nature-gov-127}}, agreed at the UN Conference on Environment and Development. The Pan-European set has 6 criteria, such as forest health and biodiversity, and the Montréal Process set has 7 criteria and 54 indicators. They also help shape forest certification standards.

nature-res-163.title: Water bankruptcy: past the point of recovery
nature-res-163.text: On 20 January 2026, a United Nations University report declared that the world had entered a global water bankruptcy era. In water bankruptcy, long overuse has damaged a water system so lastingly that it cannot return to its former supply and ecosystem services. It has two parts. Withdrawals exceed renewable inflows and safe depletion limits, and the damage cannot be undone without disproportionate cost. That sets it apart from scarcity, stress or a water crisis, which may still be reversible. Kaveh Madani formally defined it.

nature-res-100.title: Water abstraction charges: paying to take water
nature-res-100.text: In most countries, taking water straight from a river, lake or aquifer is free. Some charge a fee, called a water abstraction charge, typically to industries, utilities and farmers. Few countries outside the OECD, the club of rich economies, charge them, and where they exist fees are often nominal or poorly enforced. The biggest user escapes. Agriculture, the largest water user worldwide, is exempt in almost all countries that charge.

nature-res-162.title: Restoration hotspots: where regrowing rainforest pays most
nature-res-162.text: For an individual landowner, clearing forest often pays more than keeping it. Restoration hotspots are the places where restoring rainforest gives the highest social and economic benefits and is most feasible. Benefits are scored on biodiversity, climate mitigation, climate adaptation and water security. Feasibility weighs the {{ref:nature-econ-095}} of taking land out of farming, the forest's ability to recover and the chance it lasts. By these tests over 863 Mha of rainforest qualifies, nearly a third of it in Brazil.

nature-res-176.title: Von Thünen's rings: distance shapes the farm
nature-res-176.text: In 1826 Johann Heinrich von Thünen published The Isolated State, a model of how farmland gets used around a market. In it, the cost of hauling goods to market eats into the {{ref:nature-res-218}} land can earn, so centrality and transport decide what is grown where. It is considered the first example of marginal analysis, and an early abstract model to which mathematics could be applied. Its publication is said to mark the real start of location theory, and von Thünen has been called the father of location theorists. Critics say it oversimplified by assuming an isolated state or a single city.

nature-res-167.title: The human right to water and sanitation
nature-res-167.text: On 28 July 2010, the UN General Assembly recognized clean drinking water and sanitation as a human right. The principle is that every life depends on them. Its clearest definition came in General Comment 15 of the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, drafted in 2002. Recognition is not the same as enforcement, though. Only a few countries have written the right into enforceable law.

nature-res-165.title: Water resource policy: blue, green and grey water
nature-res-165.text: Water policy sorts water by color. Blue water is surface water and groundwater, green water is rain held in soil for plants, and grey water is water dirtied by use. Virtual water, the water hidden in traded goods, is a fourth category. Water resource policy is the policy-making and law that govern how water is collected, treated, used, disposed of and protected. It varies by region with water availability, the state of rivers and lakes, and local needs. Droughts are growing more frequent and intense with climate change, but water policy tends to react rather than plan ahead.

nature-res-166.title: Transboundary water agreements: sharing rivers across borders
nature-res-166.text: About 60% of the world's fresh water flows across political boundaries, because basins do not follow national borders. Transboundary water agreements are the treaties and other deals by which countries share and manage that water. An estimated 3600 water treaties have existed, more than 150 of them new since 1950. Geography matters. Rivers that form a border and can be shared equally tend to cause less conflict than upstream–downstream arrangements. Growing scarcity, climate change and poorer water quality have increased international conflict over water.

nature-res-172.title: The water-energy nexus: two resources tied together
nature-res-172.text: Gulf states spend 10–25% of their electricity on desalinating water. That is the water-energy nexus at work. Making energy takes water, and extracting, treating, moving, heating and disposing of water takes energy. Every form of energy needs some water, and every stage of water supply needs energy. Thermoelectric power plants, which use water for cooling, are by far the largest users. Some low-carbon options, such as biofuels, concentrating solar power, carbon capture and nuclear power, are quite water-intensive.

reviews.forests-land-and-water: Land, forests and water turn out to be one system. How land is used decides how much rain soaks into the ground, how fast rivers flood and how much carbon stays in trees. Groundwater supplies about half of the world's drinking water and 40% of irrigation water, yet pumping it faster than it refills sinks land, salts aquifers and leaves small farmers paying for deeper wells. The rules people choose shape the outcome, from prior appropriation and riparian rights to water prices, land taxes and the sustainable management of forests. Across all of it runs the same tension: the planet holds plenty of water and land, but not always where and when people need them.
